what: Zillow runs the website most Americans use to look at houses. It makes almost all of its money selling leads and software to real estate agents, mortgage brokers and rental landlords rather than from the transactions themselves. Its Zillow Showcase, rentals marketplace and mortgage origination business are the growth areas.
customers: Real estate agents who pay for buyer leads in their area, rental landlords and property managers advertising listings, mortgage lenders, and the home buyers and renters who use the site free of charge.
money: Agent advertising through Premier Agent, Showcase listings and new construction advertising.
Advertising for multifamily and single-family rental listings, the fastest-growing segment.
Zillow Home Loans origination and related services.
moat: Zillow has the audience, and in a classifieds business the audience is everything. Buyers start their search there out of habit, agents therefore have to be there, and no competitor has been able to buy that habit back. The rentals marketplace is building the same position in a market that has historically been fragmented across dozens of listing sites.
risks: The trailing period shows a net loss of about $113.0M, and the shares trade at about 53 times EV/EBITDA.
CoStar is spending very large sums on Homes.com specifically to break Zillow’s hold on the audience, and it has the balance sheet to keep doing so for years.
Revenue depends on existing home sale volumes, which have been near multi-decade lows because of mortgage rates and the resulting lock-in of homeowners on cheap loans.
The industry’s commission structure is being reshaped by litigation and settlements, and Zillow’s agent advertising model is downstream of however agents end up being paid.
Revenue fell from $2.1B in 2021 to $1.9B in 2023 before recovering, a reminder that the business is tied to a cyclical market it does not control.
opportunities: Revenue has recovered strongly, from $1.9B in 2023 to $2.6B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $2.9B, even while home sale volumes stayed weak.
Free cash flow of $313.0M against the reported loss shows the cash economics are considerably better than the earnings line, which is depressed by share-based compensation and amortisation.
Rentals is the genuinely exciting part: a large, fragmented advertising market where Zillow already has the traffic and is converting it into a second revenue engine.
Cash of $1.3B against $457.0M of debt means it can fund the fight with CoStar without raising money.
Twenty analysts average a $38.45 target, about 40% above the current price.
watch: Rentals revenue growth, and traffic share against Homes.com. The residential business will move with the housing market; the rentals engine and the audience are what determine whether Zillow is still the default in five years.
view: Zillow is a classifieds business, and classifieds businesses live and die on one thing: whether the audience still arrives by habit. For fifteen years American home buyers have opened Zillow first, which means agents have no choice but to advertise there, which funds the product that keeps buyers arriving. That loop is the whole company. Everything else — the mortgage arm, the ill-fated attempt to buy and flip houses, the software for agents — is an attempt to monetise the loop more heavily.

The reason the stock is contested is that CoStar has decided to attack the loop directly, spending extraordinary sums promoting Homes.com with an explicitly agent-friendly pitch. This is the first well-funded assault on Zillow’s audience in a decade, and CoStar has both the money and the patience to keep it up. My reading of the evidence so far is that it has not worked: Zillow’s revenue grew from $1.9 billion to $2.6 billion through a period when existing home sales were at generational lows and a competitor was carpet-bombing the category with advertising. If the audience were slipping, that could not have happened. But the fight is not over and it is expensive to defend.

What the market seems to be undervaluing is rentals. Residential advertising is tied to home sale volumes, which are currently depressed by mortgage lock-in and will recover when rates fall — that is a cyclical call anybody can make. Rentals is structural: a large, fragmented advertising market where listings have historically been scattered across dozens of sites and where Zillow already has the traffic. Building the default rental marketplace in the United States is a second business of comparable eventual size to the first, and it is growing at a rate the blended revenue figure obscures.

On the numbers: ignore the $113 million net loss, which is mostly share-based compensation and amortisation, and look at $313 million of free cash flow with $1.3 billion of net cash. At 53 times EV/EBITDA this is not cheap on any current measure, and I would not pretend otherwise — you are paying for the recovery in home sales plus the rentals build-out. The twenty analysts’ $38.45 average, about 40% up, is underwriting both. The honest framing is that Zillow is a high-quality franchise at a full price with one genuine threat and one genuine second act, and the two things to monitor are rentals revenue and audience share. If traffic holds while rentals compounds, the multiple takes care of itself.
bull: The audience holds against Homes.com, rentals becomes a second business of comparable size, and a recovery in home sale volumes arrives on top of both.
bear: CoStar’s spending gradually erodes the habit that the whole model rests on, while home sales stay frozen and a 53 times EBITDA multiple has nothing to fall back on.
